{"id": "87:10/q02", "question": "What does the future form in سَيَذَّكَّرُ convey?", "turns_on": "Whether the future marks a divine promise or the time needed for reflection.", "positions": [{"id": "87:10/q02/p1", "position": "It promises a certain future response by the fearful person.", "reasons": "Rāzī compares God's assured promise in 87:6. Biqāʿī says the promise cannot fail and extends even to subtle reminders. Baghawī, Nasafī, and Bursawī render the response as soon forthcoming."}, {"id": "87:10/q02/p2", "position": "It describes remembrance after time spent reflecting and deliberating.", "reasons": "Rāzī presents this as the alternative to an assured promise; his fuller account also records both possibilities."}]}
{"id": "87:10/q03", "question": "Why is acquiring the reminder called remembering?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "87:10/q03/p1", "position": "Clear proofs make the knowledge seem previously present, though imitation and obstinacy have obscured it.", "reasons": "Rāzī notes that remembering usually follows prior knowledge and forgetting; the clarity of the proofs explains this usage even for unbelievers."}]}
{"id": "87:10/q04", "question": "What response does سَيَذَّكَّرُ describe?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "87:10/q04/p1", "position": "The fearful person takes heed of the Quranic reminder, reflects on its truth, and accepts its guidance.", "reasons": "Ṭabarī links this to Muhammad's commanded admonition and fear of punishment; Qatāda says no servant fears God without remembering Him, and contrasts disdain for the reminder and its people. Muqātil includes affirming God's oneness, forgiveness, and freedom from reckoning. Kashshāf, Bayḍāwī, Bursawī, and Ālūsī trace reflection to truth and belief; Nasafī says acceptance. Ibn Kathīr links it to meeting God and Muhammad's message. Ibn ʿAṭiyya says learned people and believers respond according to their guidance; Ibn ʿĀshūr treats the verb as intransitive. Tabāṭabāʾī cites this verse against an interpretation of 87:14–16 that would conflict with the fearful person's remembrance."}]}
{"id": "87:10/q05", "question": "What does يَخْشَىٰ mean, and what is feared?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "87:10/q05/p1", "position": "It means fearing God, His punishment, the Hereafter, or a bad end; fear occurs in degrees.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr glosses khashya as fear, cites 20:44, and says believers differ by degree; he adds that the verb has no expressed object. Ṭabarī and Qushayrī specify God's punishment; Kashshāf and Nasafī mention a bad end; Ibn ʿAṭiyya mentions the Hereafter. Study Quran distinguishes certainty, admitted possibility, and denial of return. Corpus Coranicum cites 79:26 and Andrae's parallel of fear of the judging God and watchfulness in contemporary Christian monastic piety."}]}
{"id": "87:10/q06", "question": "Who is the one described as fearing and heeding?", "turns_on": "Whether man designates a class, a knowledge-defined subset, or an individual named by reports.", "positions": [{"id": "87:10/q06/p1", "position": "It denotes the general class of people disposed to fear God, with different degrees of receptivity.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr expressly rejects restriction to one person: man is generic and its singular form governs singular agreement; unexpressed fear lets the person weigh harm and benefit. Biqāʿī includes even innate fear and links it to felicity. Rāzī divides people into those certain of resurrection, undecided, and deniers; his broader reading includes believers and non-hostile doubters, who outnumber hostile deniers. Bayḍāwī includes the certain and hesitant; Ibn ʿAṭiyya and Abū Ḥayyān include scholars and believers in varying measure. Study Quran calls outright deniers the most wretched."}, {"id": "87:10/q06/p2", "position": "It means those whose knowledge of God and certainty of resurrection make them fearful.", "reasons": "Rāzī's narrower reading attributes fear to knowledge of God's power, knowledge, and wisdom, citing 35:28, which links fear to knowledgeable servants."}, {"id": "87:10/q06/p3", "position": "The person is ʿUthmān ibn ʿAffān.", "reasons": "ʿAṭāʾ is reported by Wāḥidī as identifying the person who takes heed; separate reports name ʿUthmān as the occasion of revelation."}, {"id": "87:10/q06/p4", "position": "The person is Ibn Umm Maktūm.", "reasons": "Al-Farrāʾ and reports through Ibn ʿAbbās identify him in the revelation account; Rāzī also records this occasion."}, {"id": "87:10/q06/p5", "position": "The person is Abū Bakr.", "reasons": "Al-Ḥusayn ibn Waqād identifies the fearful one as Abū Bakr, as reported by Naḥḥās."}]}
{"id": "87:10/q07", "question": "What occasion of revelation is reported for this verse?", "turns_on": "The reports identify different people, and one supplies the date-palm incident.", "positions": [{"id": "87:10/q07/p1", "position": "It was revealed about Ibn Umm Maktūm.", "reasons": "Wāḥidī attributes this to al-Farrāʾ; Qurṭubī gives Abū Ṣāliḥ's report from Ibn ʿAbbās; Rāzī records the alternative report."}, {"id": "87:10/q07/p2", "position": "It was revealed about ʿUthmān ibn ʿAffān.", "reasons": "Rāzī records this report. Bursawī gives the accompanying account: a hypocrite refused to exchange a date palm for one in Paradise, so ʿUthmān gave the petitioner his own orchard and the verse was revealed."}]}
{"id": "87:10/q08", "question": "Does naming the fearful exclude other people from taking heed?", "turns_on": "Whether the verse describes the strongest response or a boundary on who benefits.", "positions": [{"id": "87:10/q08/p1", "position": "Fear is singled out because it makes the response stronger, though hopeful people may also remember.", "reasons": "Māwardī states both fear and hope can prompt remembrance; Qurṭubī transmits the same explanation from him. Ibn ʿĀshūr says believers differ by their degree of fear."}, {"id": "87:10/q08/p2", "position": "Those who fear are the people who benefit from the reminder, while the wretched evade it.", "reasons": "Abū Ḥayyān and Study Quran describe benefit as limited to the fearful; Kuran Yolu points to the evasive wretched and Hell in 87:12. Qatāda contrasts the one who remembers with one who shuns the reminder out of disdain and hatred. Tabāṭabāʾī says reminder benefits the fearful by inclining them to truth."}]}
{"id": "87:10/q09", "question": "Why does fear lead a person to heed the reminder?", "turns_on": "Whether the notes emphasize reflective fear or an existing receptive disposition; they present compatible explanations.", "positions": [{"id": "87:10/q09/p1", "position": "Fear prompts reflection on the warning and its evidence, leading to recognition of truth and belief.", "reasons": "Kashshāf contrasts the unreflective and unafraid. Abū Ḥayyān says one seeks escape from what one dreads; Ibn ʿĀshūr says a person considers possible harm and benefit lest the warning apply. Bayḍāwī, Bursawī, and Ālūsī trace reflection to recognition and belief. Quṭb links a living heart's awe to knowledge of just accounting for good and evil; Biqāʿī says fear leads to every good and Paradise."}, {"id": "87:10/q09/p2", "position": "A tender heart or preserved natural light is receptive to the reminder.", "reasons": "Qāshānī names tender hearts, sound natures, and receptivity to the reminder's light and purity. Iṣlāḥī says people who preserve nature's God-given light recognize the prophet's call or awaken when prompted; where it is extinguished, only the Judgement trumpet awakens them."}]}
{"id": "87:10/q10", "question": "Whom should the Prophet remind in light of this verse?", "turns_on": "Whether the emphasis falls on a general invitation, avoiding fruitless pursuit, or tailoring its content.", "positions": [{"id": "87:10/q10/p1", "position": "He should address everyone, since the receptive are not known to him and the call itself fulfills his duty.", "reasons": "Rāzī says only God sees inward fear; many opponents merely resist verbally, most people are hesitant, warnings of the greater Fire in 87:12–13 break hearts, and forfeiting much good to avoid little evil is itself evil. Qushayrī says the caller earns reward even where only the fearful benefit. Ibn ʿĀshūr says the omitted object of 'remind' generalizes the audience; Quṭb says the Prophet fulfills his duty and God deals with each response. Corpus Coranicum, citing Robinson, says calls to the messenger can appeal generally, with him exemplary for believers."}, {"id": "87:10/q10/p2", "position": "He should remind where it is useful without pursuing or forcing the obdurate.", "reasons": "Iṣlāḥī says the fearful heed and the wretched evade, so the Prophet is to leave the evaders to their fate; their rejection reflects their condition rather than a defect in the message or preacher."}, {"id": "87:10/q10/p3", "position": "He should adapt the reminder to what matters to each hearer.", "reasons": "ʿIṣām al-Dīn says unbelievers should be called to faith before subsidiary duties, while a sinful believer may need reminding about prayer rather than faith."}]}
{"id": "87:10/q11", "question": "How does this response relate to the preceding condition about useful reminder?", "turns_on": "How to read the preceding 'if': parenthesis without converse implication, omitted alternative, temporal 'when,' or an actual limit on useful reminding.", "positions": [{"id": "87:10/q11/p1", "position": "The condition does not restrict the command: all are invited, though only some benefit.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr calls the condition parenthetical and says the outcome cannot be predicted; he cites 50:45 and says it challenges certainty of universal benefit, with Abū Jahl an example of known refusal. He adopts Ibn ʿAbbās's distinction between God's allies and enemies and rejects ellipsis. Ālūsī says a condition need not imply its converse. Rāzī says hidden fear requires general address. Study Quran also connects the preceding verse to benefit for those who fear."}, {"id": "87:10/q11/p2", "positio

n": "The command has an implicit second case: remind whether it benefits or does not.", "reasons": "Al-Farrāʾ, al-Naḥḥās, al-Jurjānī, and al-Zahrāwī propose ellipsis; Ālūsī compares 16:81, which mentions clothing protecting from heat and omits cold. Ibn ʿĀshūr reports al-Farrāʾ and al-Naḥḥās but calls the supplement unnecessary."}, {"id": "87:10/q11/p3", "position": "The particle 'in' can mean 'when,' avoiding a restrictive condition.", "reasons": "Ālūsī reports this Kūfan analysis with Quranic and hadith usage, including 3:139; other grammarians deny the sense and give alternative analyses of those examples."}, {"id": "87:10/q11/p4", "position": "The benefit condition is real because the reminder is not futile and inclines the fearful toward truth.", "reasons": "Tabāṭabāʾī explicitly treats benefit as a real condition; Iṣlāḥī reads the Prophet's task as reminding where useful."}]}
{"id": "87:10/q12", "question": "How does this verse relate to the following contrast and the surah's message?", "turns_on": "The notes describe both the immediate contrast and its place in the wider surah.", "positions": [{"id": "87:10/q12/p1", "position": "It begins the contrast between the receptive and the wretched, whose responses lead to different fates.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭiyya contrasts heeding with rejection and Fire. Quṭb says people diverge after the Prophet's reminder. Ibn ʿĀshūr says the wretched counterpart is heedless in delusion and pleasure. Iṣlāḥī describes evaders who take worldly life as all and fear no Hereafter, then face Fire without life or death and wish vainly for death. Kuran Yolu cites 87:12. Corpus Coranicum says 87:10–11 contrast responses, 87:12–15 their fates in a chiasm paralleled by 92:5–11,14–21; the good outcome balances the Hell warning."}, {"id": "87:10/q12/p2", "position": "It moves the messenger's divinely preserved revelation into public admonition within a surah about divine oneness and final recompense.", "reasons": "Corpus Coranicum says the second stanza addresses the messenger after praise, perhaps with close followers, and gives 87:6 public purpose; the warning implies fear, purification, invocation, and prayer, with 87:15 recalling 87:1. Quṭb describes the surah as a cosmic sanctuary of praise, good news of preservation and ease, and a message rooted in earlier scriptures about creation, revelation, and the afterlife; Biqāʿī adds gratitude for intellect and the faculties of heart, tongue, and limbs."}]}
{"id": "87:10/q13", "question": "What are this surah's setting and recitational use?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "87:10/q13/p1", "position": "Al-Aʿlā is Meccan, has nineteen verses, and was recited by the Prophet at Eid and Friday prayers with al-Ghāshiya.", "reasons": "Quṭb says the Prophet loved the surah and sometimes recited the two surahs on the same day."}]}
{"id": "87:10/q14", "question": "What anecdotes illustrate the choice between worldly goods and Paradise?", "turns_on": "The anecdotes describe different people, bargains, and goods.", "positions": [{"id": "87:10/q14/p1", "position": "A hypocrite refused a Paradise date palm, while ʿUthmān gave an orchard to the petitioner.", "reasons": "Bursawī connects this exchange to the verse's revelation."}, {"id": "87:10/q14/p2", "position": "One man chose eighty sheep over Paradise.", "reasons": "Bursawī tells this as one of two related stories contrasting worldly goods and Paradise."}, {"id": "87:10/q14/p3", "position": "An old woman preferred Paradise to a hundred sheep for revealing Joseph's bones to Moses.", "reasons": "Bursawī pairs her choice with the story of the man who took eighty sheep."}]}
{"id": "87:10/q15", "question": "How are people's divergent responses related to divine knowledge and human disposition?", "turns_on": "The notes emphasize divine foreknowledge or the hearer's disposition without explicitly arguing against each other.", "positions": [{"id": "87:10/q15/p1", "position": "God has always known who will accept or reject, but leaves each person's outcome unidentified as a trial and proof.", "reasons": "Biqāʿī likens the groups to those who accept treatment and those who do not, and says God establishes proof through familiar means. He also links innate fear with those destined for felicity."}, {"id": "87:10/q15/p2", "position": "Rejection reflects the evader's own condition, while acceptance reflects preserved natural light.", "reasons": "Iṣlāḥī says refusal shows no flaw in the message or preacher; people whose God-given light remains can recognize the prophet's call, while those whose light is extinguished await the Judgement trumpet. Quṭb says God deals with people according to their response."}]}
{"id": "87:11/q01", "question": "What does وَيَتَجَنَّبُهَا describe the person doing?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "87:11/q01/p1", "position": "He deliberately turns away from and refuses to receive the reminder.", "reasons": "Al-Farrāʾ says he does not remember; al-Zajjāj supplies al-dhikrā as the understood object. Jishumī explains tajannub as turning to one side from what conflicts with one. Ibn ʿĀshūr explains its form as taking a position beside something, a picture of deliberate distance. Naṣafī adds nonacceptance; Bursevī adds refusal to listen receptively. Biqāʿī says he forces his originally upright nature away from a reminder delivered by the noblest messenger. Muqātil describes slighting or neglecting monotheism. Qutb says he will neither hear nor benefit."}]}
{"id": "87:11/q02", "question": "What does the pronoun ـهَا refer to?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "87:11/q02/p1", "position": "It refers to the reminder or admonition.", "reasons": "Al-Wāḥidī attributes this to al-Farrāʾ and al-Zajjāj; Corpus Coranicum points back specifically to verse 9 and notes Paret's comparison with Q 92:17, where subject and object are reversed and the object is Hellfire."}]}
{"id": "87:11/q03", "question": "Who is ٱلْأَشْقَى, and how strong is the description?", "turns_on": "Whether the elative marks all unbelievers, a distinct extreme of hostility, the contrast between response groups, or a specific occasion; the notes also differ on whether it functions as a true superlative.", "positions": [{"id": "87:11/q03/p1", "position": "The unbeliever as a class, more wretched than a sinful believer.", "reasons": "Māwardī ties the condition to unbelief; Kashshāf, Bayḍāwī and Nasafī state the comparison with the sinner. Ṭabrisī specifies sinners who disbelieve in God and worship another. Bursevī includes all unbelievers as an alternative. Ālūsī reports this but prefers the persistent denier. Ibn ʿĀshūr says the definite article is generic and includes every polytheist; he prefers this over restriction to named men, because unbelief leads to eternal Hell. Kur'an Yolu calls them rejecters of God. The Study Quran describes them as deniers of return to God."}, {"id": "87:11/q03/p2", "position": "The particularly hostile or obstinate unbeliever, most wretched among unbelievers.", "reasons": "Kashshāf, Nasafī and Ālūsī cite deep enmity toward the Messenger; Bayḍāwī says deep immersion in unbelief. Abū Ḥayyān and Biqāʿī explain the extreme degree by rejection of Muhammad, the noblest messenger, while believers in him surpass believers in earlier messengers. Rāzī contrasts knowledgeable, hesitant and defiant hearers: the obstinate denier refuses the call and benefits from no warning. Ālūsī prefers the persistent denier of resurrection and truths that should awaken fear."}, {"id": "87:11/q03/p3", "position": "The wretched one as God already knows or has decreed him to be.", "reasons": "Thaʿlabī and Wāḥidī appeal to God's foreknowledge; Baghawī and Qurṭubī say he is wretched in God's knowledge. Ibn ʿAṭiyya calls his misery decreed and says he rejects the reminder through disbelief; his fuller account contrasts those fearing God and the Hereafter, who heed it."}, {"id": "87:11/q03/p4", "position": "The most wretched of the two response groups: those who avoid the reminder.", "reasons": "Ṭabarī says they are the party whom the reminder did not benefit and who enter the great Fire. Abū Muslim explicitly compares the fearers and avoiders. Ibn ʿĀshūr treats the definite article as marking a general class, while Qutb calls the word the absolute endpoint of wretchedness. Rāzī says an Arabic superlative need not presuppose a separate class of merely wretched people, comparing Q 25:24."}, {"id": "87:11/q03/p5", "position": "A particular named opponent or opponents.", "reasons": "Reports variously name al-Walīd ibn al-Mughīra and ʿUtba ibn Rabīʿa, sometimes adding Umayya ibn Khalaf or Abī; Ibn ʿĀshūr reports exegetes who limit the definite description to al-Walīd or ʿUtba. The differing lists and occasion reports are set out in the report question."}, {"id": "87:11/q03/p6", "position": "The unbelievers of Muhammad's community, more wretched than earlier communities' unbelievers.", "reasons": "Ālūsī reports an analogy: this community's believers are more blessed than earlier believers, so its unbelievers are more wretched; Abū Ḥayyān and Biqāʿī make the corresponding comparison concerning Muhammad's followers and rejecters."}, {"id": "87:11/q03/p7", "position": "Simply a wretched person, with the elative used like a positive adjective.", "reasons": "Rāzī reports this alternative, compares Q 30:27's use of 'easy,' and cites an Arabic poetic line for the usage."}, {"id": "87:11/q03/p8", "position": "The hypocrite in the date palm account.", "reasons": "The report through ʿAṭāʾ from Ibn ʿAbbās makes verse 11 refer to the hypocrite who refused the Prophet's offer; Qurṭubī's fuller account also reports this identification. No grading is supplied."}]}

e punishment, opposite felicity. Ibn ʿĀshūr defines its religious sense as humiliation and torment in the afterlife from unbelief and says one who dies a believer is not wretched. Corpus Coranicum notes the eschatological sense in Q 92:15 and possible threat in Q 91:12."}]}
{"id": "87:11/q05", "question": "Why does the person avoid the reminder, and how responsible is he?", "turns_on": "The notes variously stress personal choice, contempt, lack of fear, or divine foreknowledge; only Jishumī explicitly disputes determinism.", "positions": [{"id": "87:11/q05/p1", "position": "His refusal is his own blameworthy, avoidable act.", "reasons": "Jishumī says he has the capacity to do otherwise, explicitly arguing against determinist created acts and capacity. Biqāʿī says he forces his upright nature against the reminder, a sign of aversion; Islāḥī says rejection reflects the receiver's condition rather than a flaw in the message or preacher."}, {"id": "87:11/q05/p2", "position": "He lacks fear of God or the Hereafter and clings to disbelief or worldly delusion.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr says delusion and pleasure leave him seeking no escape; Ṭabāṭabāʾ contrasts him with the fearful. Islāḥī says evaders treat this life as all there is, and that loss of nature's God-given light leaves some unresponsive until the Judgement trumpet. The Study Quran contrasts deniers of return with both certain and uncertain believers who fear God. Ālūsī specifies persistent denial of resurrection or other fear-producing truths; Qutb describes a dead, dull soul anxiously preoccupied with trifles."}, {"id": "87:11/q05/p3", "position": "He shuns it out of contempt for the reminder and hatred of its people.", "reasons": "Qatāda contrasts God-fearing people who remember with those who disdain the reminder and its people; Ibn Abī Ḥātim includes hostility as well as disdain."}, {"id": "87:11/q05/p4", "position": "His wretchedness is already known to God or decreed.", "reasons": "Thaʿlabī, Wāḥidī, Baghawī and Qurṭubī phrase his state in God's foreknowledge; Ibn ʿAṭiyya says his misery was decreed. These notes do not themselves say he lacks capacity."}]}
{"id": "87:11/q06", "question": "What reports identify people or events behind the verse?", "turns_on": "The transmitted occasion or identification differs in number and identity of opponents, and one account instead concerns a hypocrite and ʿUthmān.", "positions": [{"id": "87:11/q06/p1", "position": "It was revealed concerning al-Walīd ibn al-Mughīra and ʿUtba ibn Rabīʿa.", "reasons": "The two names occur as an unnamed report in Kashshāf, Qurṭubī, Nasafī and Ālūsī; Ibn ʿĀshūr says some restrict the subject to either one. Rāzī says the wording remains general despite occasion reports."}, {"id": "87:11/q06/p2", "position": "The most wretched are ʿUtba ibn Rabīʿa, al-Walīd ibn al-Mughīra, and Umayya ibn Khalaf.", "reasons": "Al-Ḥusayn ibn Waqād supplies this three-person identification in al-Naḥḥās."}, {"id": "87:11/q06/p3", "position": "Occasion reports name al-Walīd, ʿUtba, and Abī.", "reasons": "Rāzī gives this variant list while arguing that the verse's wording applies generally and its sequence also has a rational basis."}, {"id": "87:11/q06/p4", "position": "The verse concerns a hypocrite who refused a date palm exchange for Paradise.", "reasons": "A report through ʿAṭāʾ from Ibn ʿAbbās says the Prophet offered him a tree in Paradise; ʿUthmān then gave the petitioner his orchard for the leaning date tree, and verse 14 concerns ʿUthmān. Qurṭubī gives no grading. Bursevī relates the same basic event. His related illustrations contrast a man choosing eighty sheep over Paradise with an old woman choosing Paradise over a hundred sheep for revealing Joseph's bones to Moses."}]}
{"id": "87:11/q07", "question": "What fate follows the avoidance?", "turns_on": "The notes describe both the following verses' afterlife punishment and, in Qutb, a present worldly misery.", "positions": [{"id": "87:11/q07/p1", "position": "He enters the great Fire and endures continuing punishment without restful death or beneficial life.", "reasons": "Ibn Jawzī calls it greater and more dreadful than worldly fire. Ḥasan, cited by Rāzī, identifies Hell in contrast with this world's lesser fire; other accounts distinguish levels of fire or make it the lowest level for unbelievers, with Q 4:145 on hypocrites. Ibn Kathīr relates the neither-dying-nor-living state to Q 43:77 and 35:36. Qutb says the punishment has no known end; Islāḥī says evaders wish for death in vain. Ibn ʿĀshūr says verse 12 explains the initially ambiguous description 'most wretched.'"}, {"id": "87:11/q07/p2", "position": "His earthly life is already spiritually dead, anxious, and confined to trivial concerns.", "reasons": "Qutb says the dull soul cannot perceive existence's truths or respond to its signs, before the unending afterlife punishment described in verses 12–13."}]}
{"id": "87:11/q08", "question": "How does this verse fit the surrounding passage?", "turns_on": "The notes describe different scales of structure: the immediate two-group contrast and the larger turn to public proclamation.", "positions": [{"id": "87:11/q08/p1", "position": "It contrasts fearful hearers with avoiders and pairs each response with its outcome.", "reasons": "Qutb says the Prophet delivers reminder and God deals with hearers according to response. Corpus Coranicum says verses 10–11 contrast good and bad responses, with Hell in verses 12–13 balanced by promise in 14–15; its fuller structural account calls verses 10–11 and 12–15 a chiasm, comparing Q 92:5–11 and 14–21. Biqāʿī describes reciprocal ellipsis: fear and happiness imply the second group's hard-heartedness and misery, while their cause and outcome imply the first group's opposites. Al-Mulāwī illustrates such cause-outcome correspondence with planning and operating a waterwheel. Ibn ʿĀshūr says the comparison implies the avoider does not fear."}, {"id": "87:11/q08/p2", "position": "It is part of the messenger's public admonition after the opening praise and assurance of revelation.", "reasons": "Corpus Coranicum says the second stanza again addresses the messenger: after praising God, perhaps with close followers, he turns to a wider audience, making the revelation of verse 6 public in purpose."}]}
{"id": "87:11/q09", "question": "What does the verse imply for the Prophet's practice of reminding?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "87:11/q09/p1", "position": "He should give the reminder without pursuing or forcing those who persistently evade it.", "reasons": "Islāḥī says the fearful will heed it, while the obdurate face their own fate; their rejection does not show a defect in the message or preacher. Ṭabāṭabāʾ says one reminder establishes proof for the wretched, further reminders do not help, and cites Q 53:29 for turning away. Qutb says the Prophet fulfills his duty by reminding, after which people diverge."}]}
{"id": "87:11/q10", "question": "What other Qur'anic usage illuminates ٱلْأَشْقَى?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "87:11/q10/p1", "position": "Early parallels use the elative for the damned or a threatened sinner; later passages use the positive shaqiyy.", "reasons": "Corpus Coranicum points to the damned in Q 92:15 and the Thamūd compatriot in Q 91:12, perhaps with an eschatological threat; it notes that the elative disappears from later texts, with the positive in Q 19:4, 19:32, 19:48 and 11:105. Rāzī compares Q 25:24 to show the superlative need not entail a separate comparison class, and Q 30:27 plus poetry for an elative used positively."}]}
{"id": "87:11/q11", "question": "What wider sūrah setting frames this warning?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "87:11/q11/p1", "position": "Al-Aʿlā is a Meccan sūrah of nineteen verses, moving from cosmic praise and assurance of the Prophet to warning and recompense.", "reasons": "Qutb says the Prophet loved the sūrah and recited it with al-Ghāshiya at Eid and Friday prayers, sometimes on the same day. He describes the cosmos as a sanctuary of praise, the Prophet's promised preservation and ease, and the sūrah's foundations of divine oneness, revelation, afterlife recompense, and roots in earlier scriptures (87:18–19)."}]}

{"id": "87:13/q04", "question": "Why deny life after denying death?", "turns_on": "Whether the added denial mainly excludes pleasant survival, implies no escape, or is explained as verbal antithesis.", "positions": [{"id": "87:13/q04/p1", "position": "It prevents survival in the Fire from sounding like comfortable life or an honor; their life has no benefit or relief from pain.", "reasons": "Al-Biqāʿī says immortality could otherwise sound like an extraordinary honor, while failure to purify, believe, and pray explains absence of beneficial life. {"id": "87:13/q09", "question": "How does this warning fit the sūrah's surrounding argument?", "turns_on": "The notes trace the warning's role at different scales: the immediate contrast of responses, the stanza's shift to public proclamation, or the sūrah's larger themes.", "positions": [{"id": "87:13/q09/p1", "position": "It is the fate of those who evade the Prophet's reminder, contrasted with the good who heed it.", "reasons": "Quṭb says the Prophet reminds and responses diverge.
